header.sector: Datacenter construction, cooling, racks and physical inputs
header.title: State-level permitting freezes and midterm outcomes threaten the 2028 US datacenter buildout

s01_bottom_line.text: SemiAnalysis projects 62.2 GW of US net datacenter additions in 2028, most unstarted, with Texas near 30% of the total; permitting freezes and midterm outcomes could expose roughly 30 GW (if all pause candidates win) or as little as 5.7 GW (if conditions-only candidates win). ⟨cited figures: forecast; approximate⟩
The article tells subscribers which companies are most at risk from the current pause and directs research to identify which real campuses still need the approval a candidate wants to stop.

The article frames US datacenter physical buildout as facing a policy-driven downside to 2028 timing, but quantifies only exposed GW, not the earnings or revenue impact on any listed developer, equipment or power supplier.

items.text: SemiAnalysis's model projects 62.2 GW of US net datacenter additions in 2028, most not yet started ⟨cited figures: forecast⟩
Texas accounts for close to 30% of US datacenter GW additions in 2028 ⟨cited figures: forecast; approximate⟩
If every pause-proposing candidate won, those states would contain roughly 30 GW of planned 2028 capacity ⟨cited figures: forecast; approximate⟩
If the less restrictive candidates win, exposed capacity falls to 5.7 GW ⟨cited figures: forecast⟩
If reopening waits for new rules in late summer, the Texas freeze would last close to a year — five to nine additional months versus a December restart. ⟨cited figures: forecast; approximate⟩
Tier 2 states have 1.5-2 GW of meaningful unstarted 2028 capacity where additional restrictions depend on a change in political control (Pennsylvania Senate, Oklahoma governor).

s03_transmission.text: Growing bipartisan anti-datacenter backlash drives permitting freezes (TCEQ, Oregon) and campaign platforms for moratoriums or stricter conditions.

Freezes and moratoriums could delay or block unstarted 2028 capacity, reducing GW delivered on schedule (exposure of ~30 GW to 5.7 GW depending on election outcomes). ⟨cited figures: forecast; approximate⟩
Conditions-only outcomes raise development costs (grid upgrades, cooling redesign, lost tax breaks, upfront commitments) but keep a route to approval. ⟨cited figures: approximate⟩
Delays or higher costs would affect datacenter developers', hyperscalers' and suppliers' timelines, but the article does not quantify the earnings impact.
